case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: Alice supplies a two-step test, not a definition of abstract, and its application to machine learning claims remains famously inconsistent between panels and art units.
case.holding: A claim directed to an abstract idea does not become patent-eligible by reciting generic computer implementation. Eligibility requires an inventive concept beyond the idea plus a computer.
case.case_name: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank International

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: Every AI patent runs the Alice gauntlet: examiners and accused infringers use it to strike claims that dress an algorithm in boilerplate hardware, while drafters engineer around it by claiming specific architectures and training improvements. It is the doctrinal reason so many AI patents claim methods of training rather than ideas of prediction.

reading.body:
The most consequential patent eligibility rule for AI is that adding a computer to an abstract idea is not enough: *Alice* requires an inventive concept beyond the idea itself, and that requirement falls directly on every machine learning claim filed today.

The practical effect runs through claim drafting. Because examiners and accused infringers invoke *Alice* to strike claims that wrap an algorithm in generic hardware language, patent counsel have shifted toward claiming specific architectures and concrete training improvements rather than the predictive outcomes those systems produce. That shift is legible in the population of AI patents: the doctrine is one reason so many claims describe how a model is trained rather than what it concludes.

The data record one live case citing *Alice* in an AI context, University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC, which signals active litigation but does not itself resolve how the doctrine applies to large language models or neural network architectures. The most important limitation here is the one the data names directly: *Alice* supplies a two-step test, not a definition of abstraction, and application of that test has been inconsistent across panels and patent office art units. No one reading *Alice* alone can predict with confidence which AI claims survive it.
